KEY MESSAGE 1...Yet another warm and muggy morning today with
temps in the 70s to low 80s and debris clouds from dissipating 
showers to the north and west of the area filtering into ENC. As
far as today goes, do expect any leftover debris clouds to 
dissipate later this morning with yet another hot day on tap. 
1000-850 MB thicknesses will be slightly higher today (1435-1440
m) as compared to previous days which should result in highs in
the 90s. Latest guidance suggests we at least near record high
temperatures today, though whether we reach record highs today 
will be dependent on if morning cloud cover dissipates early 
enough. See CLIMATE section for more information. 

With a front to the north slowly encroaching, moisture is 
forecast to pool out ahead of the front allowing dewpoints to 
potentially increase into the mid to upper 70s, resulting in 
widespread "feels like" temperatures of 105-110F this afternoon 
across ENC. While we toyed with the idea for an Extreme Heat 
Warning across our SW'rn zones, think the morning debris clouds 
plus afternoon shower and thunderstorm activity should preclude 
us from reaching criteria. As a result have kept the heat 
advisory in place across all of ENC. We continue to encourage 
anyone planning on spending time outdoors to stay hydrated and 
to limit exposure to the heat, if able. 

While we "cool down" as compared to today this weekend, with
frontal progression slow to occur, temps still get into the mid
80s along the OBX to low to mid 90s inland. With dewpoints 
remaining in the mid to upper 70s this weekend could see
continued heat indices around 105 F. While the footprint will 
likely be smaller, this could result in additional heat 
headlines this weekend with the greatest chance to see 
additional heat headlines across our SW'rn zones which will be 
the last to be impacted by the aforementioned front. Front will 
lift north as a warm front Sun into Mon and Mon would be our 
next best chance at more widespread heat headlines across ENC. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... Best chance to see more widespread shower and
thunderstorm activity occurs today and over this weekend with 
the approach of a frontal boundary and associated mid level 
shortwave. At the outset, have a mid level ridge centered over
the Southeast. While initially this morning we will not have 
much upper level support with a mid level shortwave still in the
Ohio River Valley riding along the periphery of this ridging, 
we should see a more active seabreeze that pushes inland later 
this morning and afternoon as winds are more S'rly as compared 
to previous days. So the seabreeze wont be pinned along the 
coast. This should result in a more active seabreeze with better
moisture and more interactions with local sound and river 
breezes as well, aiding in surface convergence. Then as we get 
into tonight a combination of the aforementioned front and mid 
level shortwave should provide additional lift for another 
round of showers and thunderstorms coming in from the north and
west. This front then likely stalls across the area on Sat 
bringing continued rounds of shower and thunderstorm activity 
before the front finally lifts north as a warm front on Sun. 
Overall this should result in continued chances for scattered 
precip over the next few days so have kept high end chance PoPs 
in the forecast. 

Pre-storm environment today and tomorrow is marginally 
conducive for strong to severe storms as well as isolated 
flooding potential, supported by both NWP and AI guidance. 
Latest guidance suggests while deep layer shear will be weak 
(generally around 20-25 kts), instability will be more than 
sufficient (MLCAPE around 2000-3000 J/kg) for strong updrafts 
along the seabreeze and aforementioned front. With moisture also
pooling ahead of the front, PWATs increase to 2-2.25" today as 
well. Activity should be mainly diurnal, although there is a 
risk of some overnight convection as upstream activity migrates 
along the sub-tropical ridge. Thunderstorm activity is forecast 
to wane in intensity and coverage as we get later into tonight, 
though with the front hanging around the area tomorrow as well 
yet another potential round for strong to severe thunderstorms 
will be possible mainly south and west of where the 
aforementioned front stalls. Strongest storms could produce wet 
microbursts, frequent lightning, and torrential rainfall given 
this environment. While not likely there is also a non-zero 
tornado threat within the strongest storms. As a result SPC has 
portions of the area under a marginal risk (level 1/5) for 
severe weather today and tomorrow. 

In addition to this, slow storm motions, upper level winds
parallel to the surface front, and ample moisture will bring a 
threat for isolated instances of flash flooding and WPC also has
the areas under a marginal risk (level 1/4) for excessive 
rainfall today and tomorrow as well. 

KEY MESSAGE 3...A second frontal boundary looks to approach 
early
